rationale: A wins because it mostly keeps its hands inside the fact box. Its strongest line, "Klarna's AI now does the work of 700 agents — and its headcount fell 20%," is a real reporter-shaped tension without pretending causality is proven. B is sharper and more newsroom-native, but "Klarna automated two-thirds of its chats. The other third got harder" smuggles in the very finding it still needs to prove. That is how founders end up pitching a clever sentence instead of a defensible story.
gaps_in_A: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" overstates the facts. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that Klarna's chatbot decides them.
"Klarna cut average chat resolution from 11 minutes to under 2 — here's how" promises a how-it-works story without supplied implementation detail, customer evidence, or escalation data.

The IPO angle is directionally right, but "leans on AI it won't fully explain" blurs two gaps: Klarna won't explain cut-versus-unfilled roles; the update does not say it refuses to explain the AI system itself.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is conservative but not the most direct handoff once these four angles exist; the real next move is pick an angle, fill the proof holes, then fit-check reporters.
gaps_in_B: "The other third got harder" is not in the update. It is a good question, not a fact; stating it as the angle headline is too clever by half.
"two-thirds of its support desk automated" overstates "two-thirds of customer-service chats" and turns a chat-volume metric into an org-design claim.
"the machine takes the two-thirds that were resolvable in minutes" invents ticket difficulty and routing logic. The facts do not say the AI took easy cases or that humans now keep only hard ones.
"Decay: 24hr" for the IPO economics angle is too hot for the supplied facts. The update says Klarna has filed to go public, but gives no filing date or same-cycle news peg.
